# Odigos

> Odigos generates OpenTelemetry from any service with no code change, and captures
> the arguments and return values of any function in live production in seconds,
> without a redeploy. It exports to any OpenTelemetry backend you already run.

## What Odigos is

Odigos is an open source, eBPF-based OpenTelemetry distribution. Point it at a Kubernetes
cluster and every service starts producing OpenTelemetry traces, metrics and logs without
anyone editing code, adding an SDK, or redeploying. It detects each service's language
automatically and instruments Go, Java, Python, .NET, JavaScript, PHP and Ruby, including
compiled Go binaries that are stripped and statically linked.

Because the data is OpenTelemetry, it goes wherever you already send telemetry: Datadog,
New Relic, Honeycomb, Grafana Cloud, Splunk, Jaeger, Tempo, Loki, SigNoz, S3, or any other
OTLP endpoint. There is no proprietary format and no lock-in. Odigos runs alongside your
existing observability stack rather than replacing it.

## What makes it different

Conventional OpenTelemetry instrumentation is decided when the code is written. Whatever
spans, metrics and log lines exist today were chosen months ago by someone who did not know
which incident was coming, so when a question turns on a value nobody recorded, the only way
to answer it is to change the code and ship a release.

Odigos decides what to capture at the moment you ask. An engineer or an AI agent can point
at any function in a running service and get back the arguments it was called with and the
value it returned, in about a second, with nothing redeployed. That closes the investigation
loop for agents: instead of opening a pull request and waiting for a deploy to obtain one
more fact, the agent queries production directly and keeps going.

## How it runs

Capture runs out of process in eBPF at under 1% CPU overhead. Nothing is loaded into the
application, so an Odigos failure cannot take a customer application down with it. Data is
governed inside the customer's own cluster: RBAC controls who may capture what and on which
workloads, and PII masking, attribute deletion and sampling run in flight before anything
leaves the cluster.

## Common questions

- Does it require code changes? No. No SDK, no annotations, no redeploy.
- What does it produce? OpenTelemetry, exported to any OTLP destination you configure.
- What is the overhead? Under 1% CPU, measured out of process across 1.04 million cores.
- Which languages? Go, Java, Python, .NET, JavaScript, PHP and Ruby, detected automatically.
- Does it replace Datadog or Grafana? No. It feeds them.
- Is it open source? Yes, Apache 2.0, with a commercial Enterprise tier.
